title: Technical MCQ Set 03: Concurrency, Trees & Networking
description: Tests Java generics & wildcards, switch/varargs traps, deadlock conditions, SQL self-joins, AVL/BST properties, and IP fragmentation.

questions.subtopic: Overloading Widening vs Boxing vs Varargs
questions.question: What does the following Java code print?
questions.explanation: Java's overload resolution priority for primitive `int` is: (1) exact match, (2) primitive widening (`long`), (3) autoboxing (`Integer`), (4) varargs (`int...`). Therefore `m(long)` wins.

questions.question: What happens when the following Java code compiles and runs?
options: Compilation error on `Object[] arr = new String[3]`
Compiles cleanly, throws `ArrayStoreException` at runtime on `arr[1] = 42`
questions.explanation: Java arrays are covariant (`String[]` is a subtype of `Object[]`), so the assignment compiles, but arrays reify their component type at runtime and throw `ArrayStoreException` when storing an `Integer` into a `String[]`.

questions.question: What is the output of this Java snippet?
questions.explanation: `static` methods are NOT overridden—they are hidden and bound at compile time to the reference type (`A.ping()` prints `A `). Instance method `pong()` is dynamically dispatched to `B.pong()`, printing `b `.

questions.question: Which statement about a `List<? extends Number>` parameter `nums` in Java is TRUE?
options: You can read elements out as `Number`, and only `null` can be passed to `nums.add(...)`
You can pass a `List<Object>` to a method expecting `List<? extends Number>`
Wildcards remove all type safety checks at compile time
questions.explanation: Per PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super), `List<? extends Number>` is a producer: reading guarantees a `Number`, while adding any non-null value is rejected at compile time because the actual list could be `List<Double>`.

questions.question: In Java 8+, where are class metadata (formerly PermGen) and local primitive variables inside a running method stored respectively?
options: Metaspace (native memory) and JVM Stack frame
questions.explanation: Java 8 replaced PermGen with Metaspace (allocated in native memory) for class definitions/metadata, while local primitive variables and object references live in each thread's JVM Stack frame.

questions.question: In classic OOP design, why does having `Square extends Rectangle` (where `setWidth` and `setHeight` independently mutate width/height) violate the Liskov Substitution Principle?
options: Because code holding a `Rectangle` expects `setWidth(5); setHeight(4);` to yield area 20, which breaks when `Square` forces width=height=4
Because Java forbids inheriting concrete setters
Because `Square` uses more heap memory than `Rectangle`
questions.explanation: LSP requires a subtype to preserve behavioral contracts expected by callers of the base type. Mutating `Square` breaks `Rectangle`'s postcondition of independent width and height.

questions.question: Table `Employees(emp_id, name, manager_id)` stores the CEO with `manager_id = NULL`. Which query returns EVERY employee alongside their manager's name (showing `NULL` for the CEO)?
options: `SELECT e.name, m.name FROM Employees e INNER JOIN Employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id`
`SELECT e.name, m.name FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN Employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id`
`SELECT e.name, m.name FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN Employees m ON e.emp_id = m.manager_id`
`SELECT e.name, m.name FROM Employees e CROSS JOIN Employees m`
questions.explanation: Matching employee `e.manager_id` to manager `m.emp_id` with `LEFT JOIN` preserves employees whose `manager_id` is `NULL` (the CEO). Reversing the `ON` condition joins subordinates instead.

questions.question: Which difference between `DELETE FROM Logs;` and `TRUNCATE TABLE Logs;` is generally TRUE in standard RDBMS engines like PostgreSQL/Oracle?
options: `DELETE` removes the table schema permanently, while `TRUNCATE` keeps rows
`DELETE` is a DML operation firing row-level triggers and logging each deleted row, whereas `TRUNCATE` is DDL that deallocates pages minimally and resets identity counters in some engines
`TRUNCATE` supports a `WHERE` clause, while `DELETE` does not
`DELETE` cannot be rolled back inside a transaction
questions.explanation: `DELETE` is DML (supports `WHERE`, logs row deletions, fires `ON DELETE` triggers, can be rolled back). `TRUNCATE` is DDL (removes all rows by deallocating data pages without `WHERE` or row-level triggers).

questions.question: When decomposing relation `R(A, B, C)` into `R1(A, B)` and `R2(B, C)`, what condition guarantees a lossless-join decomposition?
options: The common attribute `B` is a superkey of either `R1` (`B -> A`) or `R2` (`B -> C`)
questions.explanation: By Heath's theorem, decomposing R into R1 and R2 is lossless iff `(R1 ∩ R2) -> R1` or `(R1 ∩ R2) -> R2` holds in F+, i.e. the intersection `B` is a superkey of at least one decomposed table.

questions.question: Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL) guarantees conflict-serializability and avoids cascading aborts by:
options: Releasing all shared and exclusive locks immediately after each read
Holding all exclusive (write) locks until the transaction commits or aborts
Allowing dirty reads between concurrent transactions
Executing every transaction on a single CPU core sequentially
questions.explanation: In Strict 2PL, a transaction cannot release any exclusive locks until commit/abort, preventing other transactions from reading uncommitted writes (eliminating cascading rollbacks).

questions.question: If an OS enforces a global linear ordering on mutexes (all threads must lock `M1` before `M2` before `M3`), which of the four Coffman conditions for deadlock is broken?
questions.explanation: Strict total lock-ordering makes a cycle of waiting threads (`T1 waits for T2 waits for T1`) mathematically impossible, directly breaking Circular Wait.

questions.question: A 32-bit virtual address space uses 4 KB pages (`2^12` bytes). If each page table entry (PTE) is 4 bytes, what is the size of a single-level page table for one process?
questions.explanation: Virtual pages = 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 = 1M entries. Page table size = 2^20 entries * 4 bytes/entry = 4 MB per process.

questions.question: Why is switching between two kernel threads of the SAME process significantly faster than switching between two separate processes?
options: Threads share the same virtual address space (page tables / TLB entries remain valid) and open file descriptors
Threads do not have their own CPU registers or call stack
Threads never invoke the kernel scheduler
Processes cannot execute on multi-core CPUs
questions.explanation: Threads of the same process share code, heap, open files, and the virtual memory map (CR3/page directory), avoiding TLB flushes during context switch (though each thread still keeps its own stack and registers).

questions.question: An IPv4 datagram carrying a 3,000-byte TCP payload (with standard 20-byte IP header, total 3,020 bytes) traverses a link with MTU = 1,500 bytes. What is the `Fragment Offset` field value of the SECOND IP fragment?
questions.explanation: Max IP payload per 1500-byte MTU fragment = 1500 - 20 = 1480 bytes (already a multiple of 8!). Thus Fragment 1 carries bytes 0..1479 (1480 bytes). Fragment 2 starts at byte 1480; Fragment Offset is measured in 8-byte units: 1480 / 8 = 185.

questions.question: In TCP Reno, when 3 duplicate ACKs arrive (fast retransmit) while `cwnd` is 32 MSS, how do `ssthresh` and `cwnd` change?
options: `ssthresh = 16`, `cwnd` halves to `16` (plus 3 MSS inflation) and enters congestion avoidance
Connection closes immediately with TCP RST
questions.explanation: Unlike a retransmission timeout (which drops `cwnd` to 1 MSS), 3 duplicate ACKs trigger Fast Retransmit/Fast Recovery: `ssthresh` becomes `cwnd/2 = 16` and `cwnd` drops to `ssthresh` rather than 1.

questions.question: Inserting keys `10, 20, 15` in that exact order into an empty AVL tree triggers which rotation at root `10`?
options: Right-Left (RL) double rotation, resulting in `15` as the new root
Left-Right (LR) double rotation, resulting in `20` as the new root
questions.explanation: 10 -> right child 20 -> left child 15 creates a Right-Left imbalance at 10. Right-rotating 20-15 then left-rotating at 10 promotes 15 to the root with left=10 and right=20.

questions.question: When implementing a FIFO Queue using two stacks (`inStack` and `outStack`, transferring only when `outStack` is empty), what is the AMORTIZED time complexity of `enqueue` and `dequeue`?
options: `O(1)` amortized for both enqueue and dequeue
`O(N)` amortized for both enqueue and dequeue
questions.explanation: Each element is pushed to `inStack` once, popped/pushed to `outStack` at most once, and popped from `outStack` once (at most 4 stack ops per element), yielding O(1) amortized per operation.

questions.question: When inserting 10,000 rows in JDBC via `PreparedStatement`, why does `addBatch()` + `executeBatch()` outperform calling `executeUpdate()` 10,000 times?
options: It bypasses database transaction logs completely
It reduces network round-trips between the Java app and the database server
It skips primary key uniqueness checks
It executes SQL inside the JVM without a database connection
questions.explanation: Calling `executeUpdate()` per row incurs 10,000 separate network round-trips; batching packs hundreds/thousands of bound parameter sets per round-trip.

questions.question: Why should you prefer `StringBuilder` over `StringBuffer` for building strings inside a single-threaded local method?
options: `StringBuilder` avoids synchronized method lock overhead on `append()`, making it faster in single-threaded code
questions.explanation: `StringBuffer` synchronizes its methods for thread safety; `StringBuilder` provides the exact same API without synchronization overhead for single-threaded usage.

questions.question: In the V-Model of SDLC, which testing phase directly validates the High-Level / Architectural Design phase?
questions.explanation: In the V-Model: Low-Level/Module Design <-> Unit Testing; High-Level/Architecture Design <-> Integration Testing; System Specs <-> System Testing; Business Requirements <-> UAT.

questions.explanation: Traditional `case:` labels fall through until hitting a `break`. Matching `case 2` prints `2`, falls through into `case 3` printing `3`, and stops at `break`.

questions.question: How do you safely compute `revenue / NULLIF(clicks, 0)` in SQL when `clicks` can be `0`, returning `0` instead of a division-by-zero error?
questions.explanation: `NULLIF(clicks, 0)` returns `NULL` when `clicks == 0`, turning `revenue / NULL` into `NULL` (avoiding division-by-zero), and outer `COALESCE(..., 0)` converts that `NULL` to `0`.

questions.question: Why must deleting a key in an open-addressed hash table (linear probing) mark the slot with a 'tombstone' (`DELETED`) sentinel rather than resetting it to `EMPTY`?
options: Resetting to `EMPTY` would double the array size immediately
Resetting to `EMPTY` would prematurely terminate future lookup probe chains for keys inserted past that slot
Tombstones reduce hash collisions to zero
Open addressing cannot store integer keys without tombstones
questions.explanation: Linear probing stops searching when it hits an `EMPTY` slot. Turning a deleted middle slot into `EMPTY` breaks the probe path for keys that collided and probed past it.

questions.question: What is the key behavioral difference between a Mutex and a Binary Semaphore?
options: A Mutex has ownership: only the thread that locked it should unlock it, whereas any thread can signal (`V()`) a Semaphore
A Binary Semaphore supports priority inheritance while a Mutex never does
A Mutex can allow up to 10 threads into a critical section simultaneously
Semaphores work only inside Java, whereas Mutexes work only in Python
questions.explanation: A mutex enforces thread ownership (lock/unlock by the same thread, enabling priority inheritance), whereas a binary semaphore acts as a signaling flag that one thread can wait on and another thread can post.

questions.question: Which DNS record type maps an alias domain (such as `www.example.com`) to another canonical domain name rather than directly to an IPv4 address?
questions.explanation: `CNAME` (Canonical Name) aliases one hostname to another hostname; `A` maps to IPv4, `AAAA` maps to IPv6, and `MX` specifies mail exchange servers.
